text: Fine-tuning a pretrained language model on a few hundred labelled examples gives much higher text classification accuracy than training a classifier from scratch. The gain is largest when fewer than 200 labelled examples are available.

Data augmentation by synonym replacement and back translation improves macro-F1 on small sentiment classification datasets. However, the improvement disappears when the training set grows beyond a few thousand examples.
Contrastive pretraining of sentence embeddings improves few-shot text classification compared with standard fine-tuning when only a handful of labelled examples per class are available.
Few-shot fine-tuning is unstable across random seeds. Reported gains over standard fine-tuning are often within the variance between seeds, so single-run comparisons can mislead.

Self-training with pseudo-labels on unlabelled text improves classification accuracy when the initial classifier is reasonably accurate. When the initial classifier is weak, pseudo-label noise can hurt performance and degrade results.
Prompt-based classification with a pretrained language model reaches competitive accuracy with only a few labelled examples, reducing the need for large labelled datasets.

Comparisons of low-resource text classification methods often use different labelled subsets, different numbers of seeds and different tuning budgets, which makes reported improvements hard to compare fairly.
Data augmentation did not give consistent gains for pretrained language models on topic classification, and in several settings the augmented models were worse than the plain fine-tuned baseline.
Reporting macro-F1 rather than accuracy is important for imbalanced text classification datasets, because accuracy can stay high while minority classes are classified poorly.
Pseudo-label self-training improved few-shot sentiment classification with a pretrained encoder, with gains reported over supervised fine-tuning on the same labelled examples.
